Ictal fear is a recognized temporal lobe seizure semiology and is easily mistaken for panic attacks; panic attacks last longer and lack automatisms, amnesia and postictal confusion.
A normal routine EEG, here with benign variants (wicket spikes, small sharp spikes), does not exclude epilepsy; video-EEG captured five habitual seizures with right anterior temporal onset.
The 3T epilepsy-protocol MRI shows subtle right temporal pole gray-white blurring suspicious for focal cortical dysplasia, concordant with the EEG onset.
She has never taken an antiseizure medication: the treatment failure was of panic therapy, so first-line monotherapy is the next step.

general.query: focal epilepsy in adults: definition, classification, imaging and first-line treatment

results.finding: Epilepsy is present after at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, after one unprovoked seizure with a recurrence risk of at least 60% over the next 10 years, or when an epilepsy syndrome is diagnosed.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2014;55:475-482 | ILAE official report: a practical clinical definition of epilepsy

results.finding: Seizures are classified by onset as focal, generalized or unknown; focal seizures are described by awareness and by their first motor or non-motor feature, and may evolve to focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.
results.source: Fisher RS et al., Epilepsia 2017;58:522-530 | Operational classification of seizure types by the International League Against Epilepsy: position paper of the ILAE Commission for Classification and Terminology

results.finding: A harmonized epilepsy MRI protocol (3D T1 and 3D FLAIR at about 1 mm isotropic resolution and high-resolution coronal T2) is recommended for adults with focal epilepsy; non-dedicated protocols miss subtle lesions.
results.source: Bernasconi A et al., Epilepsia 2019;60:1054-1068 | Recommendations for the use of structural magnetic resonance imaging in the care of patients with epilepsy: a consensus report from the International League Against Epilepsy Neuroimaging Task Force

results.finding: Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is offered as first-line monotherapy for focal seizures, with carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, zonisamide or lacosamide as further options.
results.source: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence, NG217 2022 | Epilepsies in children, young people and adults

results.finding: Drug-resistant epilepsy is failure of adequate trials of two tolerated, appropriately chosen and used antiseizure medication schedules to achieve sustained seizure freedom.
results.source: Kwan P et al., Epilepsia 2010;51:1069-1077 | Definition of drug resistant epilepsy: consensus proposal by the ad hoc Task Force of the ILAE Commission on Therapeutic Strategies

general.summary: Epilepsy is diagnosed after two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart or one with a high recurrence risk, and focal seizures are classified by onset and awareness (ILAE 2014, 2017). A dedicated epilepsy-protocol MRI is the imaging of choice (ILAE 2019). Lamotrigine or levetiracetam is first-line monotherapy for focal seizures (NICE NG217), and drug resistance is failure of two appropriate medication schedules (ILAE 2010).

patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Montoya is a 29-year-old right-handed elementary school teacher who presents for inpatient evaluation of recurrent paroxysmal episodes that have been diagnosed as panic attacks over the past two years but have been escalating in frequency and are now occurring daily despite adequate treatment with sertraline and as-needed lorazepam. She describes the episodes as beginning with a sudden, overwhelming surge of fear that she describes as unlike normal anxiety, as though something terrible is about to happen but she cannot identify what. This is accompanied by a peculiar sensation she struggles to articulate, describing it variously as her stomach flipping, a wave of warmth rising from her abdomen to her chest, and occasionally a strange smell that she says is like burning rubber that nobody else around her can detect. During some episodes she experiences a profound feeling of depersonalization, as though the world around her has become unfamiliar and dreamlike.

The episodes typically last between 30 seconds and two minutes. Her boyfriend has witnessed several and reports that during the more intense ones, she stops speaking mid-sentence, stares vacantly, and appears to chew or smack her lips. She has no memory of these observed behaviors and initially denied they occurred until he recorded one on his phone. Following the more prolonged episodes she feels confused and exhausted for 10 to 20 minutes. She has never had a convulsive episode or lost consciousness in a dramatic fashion.

She was evaluated by her primary care physician who increased her sertraline from 50 mg to 100 mg and referred her to psychiatry. Her psychiatrist diagnosed refractory panic disorder and added lorazepam. A cardiologist evaluated her palpitations and attributed them to her known mitral valve prolapse and anxiety, obtaining a normal Holter monitor. Over the past three months, the episodes have increased from weekly to near-daily, occurring unpredictably during work, rest, and even during sleep on at least two occasions where her boyfriend observed her sitting up in bed, staring, and making repetitive hand movements. She has taken medical leave from teaching because an episode occurred in front of her students. She is now referred to neurology for further evaluation after her psychiatrist questioned whether these could be epileptic in nature.
